name: Compound heterozygotes: cis or trans
description: Two damaging hits in one gene — whether they sit on opposite copies, which leaves no working copy, or on the same one, which leaves the gene intact.

script.text: Compound heterozygotes: two damaging hits in one gene, and the question of whether they sit on opposite copies or the same one.
In trans — one hit on each copy — leaves no working copy, which for a recessive condition is the genotype that causes it. In cis leaves an intact gene: a carrier.
It needs two things: a phased VCF, and the loss matrix — the list of genes this genome carries a damaging change in.
Analyze, then Find the losses. Calculate loss matrix is the step before this one; it reads every exonic variant and takes a minute on a whole genome.
Every gene with more than one damaging hit, grouped by what the phase actually settles.
Both copies hit, in trans: the two hits are in the same phase set, on opposite copies. ACMG calls that PM3 when the other variant is already known to be pathogenic.
One copy intact, in cis: both hits on the same copy, so the other copy still works — a carrier rather than a patient. ACMG BP2.
Not settled by this file: the hits are in different phase sets, or one of them is unphased. Phase only compares within one set — a parent's sequence, or reads long enough to span both, decides it.

Open any gene for each hit with its genotype, phase set and consequence, and take the whole table away as CSV. It reads phase and consequence — it does not judge pathogenicity or whether the gene fits the presentation.
